Evidence hearing · Module 11

References, Provenance, Authority, and Time

A graph becomes trustworthy when it can answer more than “what does this statement say?” It must also answer “where did it come from, who had authority, when did it apply, what transformed it, and what superseded it?” This hearing puts conflicting utility claims on the record.

Hearing
Conflicting source claims

Which Pump P-104 operating limit controls at 9:15 a.m.?

Historian extraction

Maximum discharge pressure: 115 psi

Recorded at 9:14 a.m.; extracted at 9:15 a.m.; approved range not stated.

Scanned 2018 procedure

Normal upper target: 110 psi

OCR confidence 0.91; marked superseded in the document system.

Approved 2026 operating procedure

Normal upper target: 105 psi

Effective July 1, 2026; approved by operations; applies to this pump configuration.

Operator note

“We ran near 108 last week.”

Entered yesterday; describes experience, not an approved limit.

Question before the utility

Do not pick the newest timestamp

The newest record may describe an observation. The controlling statement needs applicable authority, effective time, version, and scope.

Foundation lens: A source tells you where a statement came from. Authority tells you why it may control a decision. Those are related but not identical.

Practitioner lens: Represent entities, activities, agents, derivations, generation time, version, effective intervals, and named graph boundaries. Keep observed, recorded, extracted, and effective time separate.

Leader lens: Establish who can approve definitions and limits, how supersession works, and which conflicts force human review. Technology can rank evidence only after policy is explicit.

Rule on admissibility

Select the statement that should control the answer in this scenario. Then notice why “most recent record” is too crude: observation, entry, extraction, approval, and effective time answer different questions.

1
Evidence vocabulary

Reference, provenance, and authority answer different questions

A reference helps someone locate the supporting material. Provenance explains the statement's history. Authority explains why a statement may control a particular decision.

W3C PROV-O provides terms for an entity, an activity, and an agent. In our case, the approved procedure is an entity, the approval workflow is an activity, and the operations authority is an agent. An OCR text can be marked derived from the scanned document.

Supersession is a governance decision, not just a later timestamp. Version allows a reviewer to reproduce what the system knew. Effective time answers when it governs.

Keep the claim separate from its evidence: “P-104 has a 105 psi normal target” is one statement. “Procedure OP-26-041 says so, approved by Operations, effective July 1, version 3” is the evidence and governance surrounding it.

3
Four-clock review

“When?” is four questions, not one

A utility answer can change when you switch clocks. Observation time is when the real-world measurement occurred. Record time is when a system stored the statement. Extraction time is when a pipeline or model produced a derived representation. Effective time is when a rule or statement governs the decision.

If an inspection was observed Monday, entered Wednesday, corrected Friday, and made effective after approval the following Monday, “the latest record” is not enough. A graph can preserve all four relationships instead of forcing them into one overloaded date column.

Change the question, then change the clock

The table distinguishes the four jobs. The time lens then asks you to choose the clock that answers each question. Read the explanation after every selection.

Evidence FAQ

Questions about trust, reference, and time

Is the newest statement always the authoritative one?

No. Newest by record or extraction time may be an observation, a draft, or a derived claim. Authority depends on source role, approval, scope, effective interval, version, and supersession policy.

Is a citation the same as provenance?

No. A citation points to supporting material. Provenance can also describe extraction, transformation, attribution, generation, and derivation. Good evidence packages often need both.

Can a person’s note be authoritative?

Yes, within a defined role and scope. An operator may be authoritative for an observed field condition but not for changing an engineering limit. State what the person is authorized to establish.

How should OCR confidence affect authority?

Confidence describes the extraction, not the authority of the underlying document. A highly confident extraction from a superseded procedure should not control. A low-confidence extraction from an authoritative document should trigger review.

Why preserve superseded statements?

They support historical reconstruction, audits, incident review, and explanation of past decisions. Mark them with scope and time so they are not mistaken for current control.

Can provenance make a generative answer deterministic?

No. It can ground claims, constrain evidence selection, and improve reproducibility. Generative wording may still vary. Deterministic rules and checks should handle requirements that must not vary.

Evidence boundary

The pressure-limit hearing is instructional. It does not define an operating limit or authority policy. Local records, document-control rules, regulatory requirements, effective dates, and named operational authority must be verified. PROV-O provides provenance vocabulary, but utility governance determines which sources control which decisions.
